cultivar: AV2 and other clonals; China-type bushes
processing: Orthodox Darjeeling black tea, with much of its reputation resting on clonal and China-bush lots; first flush is lightly oxidised, as usual in Darjeeling.
harvest_season: Follows the Darjeeling flushes; the first flush of spring is the usual prize, and the second flush follows in early summer.
appearance_dry: As with other clonal Darjeeling first flushes, a light mix of green and silver-tipped leaf.
appearance_liquor: A pale golden amber in first flush, deepening in later flushes, as is usual in Darjeeling.
appearance_wet: Typically bright green leaf with coppery edges in first flush.
taste_profile: Few independent notes exist; as with other clonal Darjeeling first flushes, expect a floral, fresh and lightly brisk cup.

brewing.notes: General first flush guidance: water a little off the boil, no milk, and a shorter steep than you would give a stronger black tea.

vintage_note: Sold by year and flush with a lot name, often a clonal one such as Clonal Queen or Clonal Superb. First flush lots are at their best within a year or so of picking, and it pays to compare individual lots rather than rely on the estate name.
description:
Puttabong, also written Pattabong and formerly called Tukvar, is one of the largest gardens in Darjeeling, with 4.37 square kilometres under tea out of 8.92 in total. The name is usually explained as meaning house of green leaves.

The garden is known for clonal lots alongside its older China-type bushes. Its Clonal Queen is linked to the AV2 cultivar, one of the better-known clones in modern Darjeeling, and lots like these are sold under their own names.

For a first flush, use water a little below boiling and go easy on the time. As with other Darjeeling clonals, expect flowers and freshness, not malt, and leave the milk out.

When buying, look for the year, flush and lot name. Also, don't mix it up with North Tukvar: it is a separate garden with the same owner and a similar name.
history:
Puttabong is dated to 1852, when a Dr Campbell is credited with planting it. Its owner, Jay Shree Tea, calls it the first tea estate in Darjeeling's history, which is a company claim rather than a settled fact.

It was formerly known as Tukvar and took its present name later. It is now part of the Jay Shree group.
